messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus Eze was forty-eight when the pressurized containment tank at the municipal waste facility ruptured. He had been kneeling beside a corroded valve, wrench in hand, when a high-pressure hiss tore through the bay. Within seconds, a thick, antiseptic-chemical vapor flooded the workspace, burning his eyes and tightening his chest. He remembered the visceral panic of suffocating on the concrete floor while his supervisor dragged him to the airlock, his lungs clawing for air that wasn’t there. The incident resolved without permanent damage, but the memory took root. Over the following weeks, Marcus noticed his body had rewritten its safety protocols. When the antiseptic smell of hospital-grade floor cleaner drifted past the bay door, or when the sharp clang of a steel tool drawer echoed through the workplace, he would instantly feel his threat detection spike. Those sensory cues bypassed his reasoning and forced a surge of alarm; his eyes darted to every corridor, his shoulders tensed, and his mind compulsively mapped every possible escape route before his feet even touched the next floor. He had come to believe that his lungs were still structurally compromised, that another unseen leak could drop him without warning, so every ordinary sound or scent became a sudden, potent trigger. To manage the escalating tension, Marcus adopted routines that kept him moving. Whenever the hospital smell or a loud noise threatened to pull him back into that suffocating panic, he responded by immediately refusing to be alone. He started leaving his house before dawn, lingering in crowded break rooms, and throwing himself into extra shifts at the disposal unit. Overwork became his anchor; he was certain that staying busy was the only way to keep the intrusive memories from pooling in the quiet of his living room. He also stopped going to occupational health clinics, avoiding physical examinations and any medical cues that reminded him of the chemical exposure. These strategies were not calculated decisions but urgent, reflexive habits that formed over months of failed attempts to sleep. The disposal bay, with its concrete floors and industrial ventilation, became the very environment that first poisoned him, and it is exactly where his triggers now fired most reliably. Yet this avoidance of empty rooms and medical settings, combined with his relentless overcompensation, ensured his nervous system never received the signal to downshift. The constant state of forced activity and crowded environments only fed back into his threat monitoring, keeping his eyes sharp, his breathing shallow, and his escape routes constantly rehearsed. His professional background as a bomb disposal technician had once rewarded hyper-vigilance, but now it sustained a chronic state of alarm. Marcus found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, his eyes tracking every shadow and ventilation shaft until his neck ached. This relentless monitoring kept his threat detection system in a permanent state of readiness, which meant that everyday workplace sounds—a dropped wrench, a pneumatic drill, a sudden footstep—now snapped into acute triggers, forcing his heart to hammer against his ribs. When a coworker clapped him on the shoulder or a stranger brushed past him in the corridor, Marcus reacted with immediate alarm, jerking away as if expecting a live wire. The fear was not of death itself, but of being caught off guard, of losing control the moment he had been helpless in that chemical bay. The cycle tightened relentlessly: his scanning kept him primed for danger, the priming magnified his triggers, the triggers demanded avoidance and overwork, and the avoidance and overwork guaranteed his threat system never rested. Now sixty-two, Marcus’s life has narrowed into a carefully choreographed circuit of vigilance and exhaustion. His marriage has weathered the strain of his chronic absences and his wife’s frustration with his inability to simply sit and rest, but he cannot break the pattern. He sought counseling only because the physical toll of sleeping two hours a night, his hands trembling during delicate disposal work, and the growing fear that he might finally panic in a crowd had become unbearable. What he hoped for was a way to breathe without waiting for the other shoe to drop, a quiet confidence that the air in any room was safe, and a restoration of the steady, grounded calm he once commanded behind the protective gear. He needed to know that the past could not leak into his present, and that he could finally lay down his watch.
